title: It's the end of the world as we know it, per a physicist's 1960 prediction
gist: Pegged to the November 13, 2026 'doomsday' date from Heinz von Foerster's 1960 Science paper (and a coincident Microsoft outage), the piece explains why extrapolating past exponential population trends failed: birth rates fell, and the global birth rate is now slightly under half its 1960 level. It then catalogs a long history of failed doomsday predictions.

insights.claim: Physicist Heinz von Foerster published a 1960 paper in Science predicting that human overpopulation would reach a breaking point on November 13, 2026, with population growth heading toward infinity.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A canonical case of trend extrapolation failing, useful as a caution for any exponential-growth forecast.

insights.claim: Von Foerster accurately measured past population trends but, like Malthus, wrongly assumed those trends would continue largely unchanged into the future.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Models fit to history can be precise and still wrong at the inflection point.
insights.locator: Population dynamics are notoriously tricky to calculate

insights.claim: Von Foerster's model projected population better than most demographers through the 1970s and 1980s, and only around 1993 did global population begin falling behind its forecasts.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Forecast accuracy over a long window does not guarantee validity; regime changes can arrive decades later.
insights.quote: Its core equation yielded projections that were better than those of most demographers throughout the 1970s and 1980s.
insights.locator: The doomsday idea persisted in part

insights.claim: The forecast faltered partly because the world did what von Foerster and colleagues recommended, making it a self-defeating prophecy; today the global birth rate is slightly less than half the 1960 rate.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Halved birth rates underpin long-run demographic headwinds relevant to labor supply and growth assumptions.
insights.quote: Today, the global birth rate is slightly less than half the 1960 rate.

insights.claim: According to Joel Cohen of Rockefeller University and Columbia University, the all-time peak in population growth occurred in the early 1960s, just as von Foerster published.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Population growth rates have been decelerating for ~60 years, a structural demographic trend.
insights.quote: He got the picture right just as that picture ceased to be right,

insights.claim: Von Foerster failed to foresee the effects of longer life expectancy and sharply declining child mortality on population dynamics.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Omitted variables, not bad math, are what break long-range models.

insights.claim: Thomas Malthus's 1798 prediction that population would outstrip food rested on exponential growth, which holds only under narrow conditions such as controlled lab bacteria cultures and never continues forever.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Exponential assumptions should be stress-tested for saturation in any growth thesis.

insights.claim: No doomsday prediction has come true yet, from religious figures like Martin Luther and Cotton Mather to scientists like Jacob Bernoulli and John Gribbin's 1974 'The Jupiter Effect'.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Base rates for catastrophic-end predictions are zero; apocalyptic narratives deserve heavy skepticism.
insights.quote: There hasn’t been a successful doomsday prediction yet.
